segments.text: Adding a package to your Flutter project is  fairly straightforward. But there's a lot
more to Pubspec and dependency management  than simply using the 'flutter pub add'
command. As your Flutter project evolves,  you'll need to use many of the additional
features and commands of pubspec and the Pub  package manager. If you're new to Flutter,
then this will be a high ROI video. In this video,  we'll cover the ins and outs of the pubspec.yaml
file and the Pub package manager. You'll flatten  your learning curve and learn the most important
Pub and pubspec concepts in under 10 minutes.  By establishing a solid foundation up front,
you'll save considerable time in  the future. Alright, let's jump in.
We'll start by creating a new Flutter  project and then open it in VSCode.
The pubspec file performs three functions: storing  basic metadata, managing assets, and managing
packages and dependencies. The first handful  of lines at the top of the file contain project
metadata including the project name, description,  a publish_to field, and a version number. This is
useful information that can help developers gain  an understanding of the details of a project. More
importantly, if you decide to publish your code  and make it available as a package on the Pub
package repository, this metadata is required.  We haven't talked about packages and Pub yet,
but for now, it's enough to know that it's  possible to share Flutter code as a package,
and in order to do so, a pubspec.yaml file  containing this data is required. The second,
and most important use of the pubspec file is  managing packages and dependencies. So what
exactly does that mean? The Flutter ecosystem  has a thriving community that shares thousands
of libraries of code, known as packages, that  can help you extend the capabilities of your
app. These range from font management tools  to audio players that you can drop in your
app. When packages are added to pubspec.yaml,  they become a dependency for a given project
because the project now depends on that package  to function properly. The Pub package manager is
a command-line tool that is used to download and  manage the packages used by our Flutter app. Let's
use the Pub command to add a package to our app.  In VSCode I'll open up the terminal panel at the
bottom. In the project folder, we'll type 'flutter  pub add' followed by a package name. Let's go with
the just_audio package. So we'll type 'flutter pub  add just_audio' and hit enter. When we run this
command Pub updates the pubspec file by adding the  just_audio dependency in the dependencies section.
In VSCode, whenever pubspec.yaml is updated,  the 'flutter pub get' command is triggered. The
'flutter pub get' command downloads the package  and related files from the Pub package repository.
These package files are not stored within the  Flutter project itself. Instead, they are placed
in a hidden directory named '.pub-cache' in your  home folder. This approach saves space by only
storing a package once, even if multiple projects  use the same package. Removing a package is quite
simple: just delete the package reference from  pubspec.yaml and save the file. This time the
opposite happens: dependencies are removed instead  of being added. It's really important to point out
that if a dependency is removed from a Flutter  project, the package itself is removed, but
any code that references the package will remain  until it's manually removed. If you're removing a
dependency from a project, it's a really good idea  to thoroughly test your app to ensure it functions
properly. Using the 'flutter pub add' command  is the easiest way to add a package to a Flutter
project. All you need to know is the package name  and Pub will fetch the appropriate version number
and add it to pubsspec. But it's possible to add a  package without using 'flutter pub add'. Instead,
you can manually add the package name to pubsspec  and save it. Let's add the Google Fonts package.
We can type the package name followed by the  ':' symbol. if we don't know the version number,
we can leave it blank and Pub will grab the  latest version. But this is generally not
recommended. When I save the file, 'flutter pub  get' is triggered and the package is downloaded.
There are times when a dependency is  required in your project but should
not be included in the final production  build. These packages should be placed
in the dev_dependencies section. Testing  frameworks and document generators are
great examples of dev dependencies. The  dependencies section on the other hand,
is intended to contain the packages that are  necessary at runtime. Including non-run time
packages in the dev_dependencies section minimizes  the size of the final build of your project.
So I already happened to know of the  Google Fonts and Just Audio packages,
but what if someone isn't familiar with these  packages? How would they know how to find them?
We can use the Pub.dev package repository to  easily browse and search for Dart and Flutter
packages. Let's do a search for 'fonts'. Notice  that there are over 1,200 packages available. Next
to each result is useful information including  the number of likes, Pub points, and popularity.
These data points can be helpful when evaluating  a package. I'll click on google_fonts. You'll
notice that there's a ton of information on  the package's features and how to implement
it. You can click on the 'installing' tab on any  package to learn how to install it. In most cases,
you'll use the 'flutter pub add' command to add  the package as a dependency to your project.
You might have noticed that the version numbers  for the packages we've added to our project are
pretty elaborate. They usually start with a caret  symbol and contain multiple dots. So what's going
on here? The three numbers separated by the dots  represent the major version, the minor version,
and the patch number. This is known as semantic  versioning. The caret symbol at the beginning
means that patching updates are allowed. This  is known as a version constraint. We can use
the tilde character instead of the caret to allow  minor version updates. The greater than and equal
to characters can be used to specify the minimum  version allowed, so any new version of a package,
as long as it's greater than or equal to  the version listed, will be updated when
an update is available. In general, the caret  is a safe choice when specifying a package
version. So if version 6.2.2 of google_fonts  is released, the next time 'pub get' is run,
the google_fonts package will be updated. However,  if version 6.3.1 or version 7.0.0 is released,
neither one will be updated because these are  minor and major updates and not a patch update.
So, as mentioned, when we add a package to our  project, it becomes a dependency of the project.
But oftentimes, the packages we install will  in turn depend on a number of other packages in
order to function properly. When 'flutter pub  get' is run, the Pub package manager resolves
these dependencies automatically. All of  these sub-dependencies are added to the
pubspec.lock file. If we take a closer look at the  pubspec.lock file, we'll see that there are quite
a few packages listed here. This is the exhaustive  set of dependencies required by our project. It's
important to note that the pubspec.lopck file  uses precise version numbers for each package,
whereas in pubspec.yaml, it's more common to  see a version range. pubspec.lock should not
be edited. This file is managed by Pub and is  updated each time changes are made to pubspec.
So far the packages that we've worked with  have been installed as local dependencies.
This means that if we want to use one of these  packages in another project on our machine,
we'd need to install it in that project as  well. A global package on the other hand is
available to all apps on a computer.  Typically command-line tools such as
flutter_fire or webdev are set up as global  packages. Let's install the webdev package.
Notice in the installation instructions, instead  of 'pub add webdev' we use 'pub global activate
webdev'. This indicates the package is being  installed globally. You'll also notice that
the installation instructions call for 'dart  pub' instead of 'flutter pub. The 'flutter pub'
command is basically an alias for 'dart pub' and  will do the same thing. You can use either one.
One last but important point on global  packages: the vast majority of packages
you'll use for your Flutter projects  are intended to be installed as local
dependencies and can't be installed as a global  package. This means you can't install a package
such as the google_fonts package as a global  package, even if you intend to use it on every
Flutter project on your machine. You'll need  to install the package within each project.
The pubspec file is also used to manage  local assets such as images icons,
audio clips, and video clips. Assets are  added to a Flutter project by declaring
them in the 'assets' section. The default  pubspec file contains a few examples that
have been commented out. Let's uncomment  one to add an image asset to our project.
Notice that when we save the pubspec  file, we receive a warning from VSCode.
This is happening because an asset has been  declared but the file itself does not exist.
Assets are typically placed in an 'assets'  folder in the root of the Flutter project.
This folder does not exist in the default  Flutter project and needs to be created.
Once we create the folder, add the asset, and save  the file, the warning disappears. You can name
this folder whatever you'd like, but 'assets' is a  common choice. If your project contains many asset
files, you can create additional subfolders  such as 'images', 'audio', and 'video'.
For large projects, listing each asset file  can be tedious and error prone. Instead,
you can simply add the folder  name to the assets section.
Alright, we've covered a lot in a short period of  time. The concepts we've explored in this video
were meant to give you a deeper understanding of  the pubspec.yaml file and dependency management.
While not exhaustive, the topics we've explored  will cover the vast majority of pubspec related
tasks you'll need to perform. If you found  this guide helpful, please give it a thumbs up,
and subscribe for more flutter tutorials. Don't  hesitate to drop your questions or topics you'd
like me to cover in the comments below. Happy  coding and I'll see you in the next video!
